english_narration: April twelfth, nineteen eighty-two. Four in the morning, at Vostok Station, in the middle of Antarctica. Outside, it is far below minus fifty-five. In eleven days, the sun will set for four months.
A power technician wakes up to smoke. The power station is on fire. In about fifteen minutes, the whole building is burning. The fire extinguishers barely work.
By morning, the station has no electricity, no heating, and no power to melt snow for water. One man is dead. Twenty are left alive.
And nobody can come for them. Not for seven months.

Vostok is where the coldest air temperature ever measured on Earth was recorded: minus eighty-nine point two Celsius. That's minus a hundred and twenty-eight Fahrenheit. People have wintered there almost every year since nineteen fifty-seven. So how do people survive at the coldest place ever measured?
The obvious answer is technology: power plants, heating. But in nineteen eighty-two, those twenty men lost all of it, and they still got through the winter.
The second answer: rescue. If something goes wrong, you fly people out. But at Vostok, for about nine months a year, no plane or tractor is supposed to come at all.

So it's something else. First, why here. Then, what this place does to a body and to a machine. Then we'll go back to the night of the fire. And at the end, we'll see the lesson Vostok learned from it, which is still shaping the station right now.

In the nineteen fifties, the world's scientists planned the International Geophysical Year. America took the South Pole. So the Soviet Union took the two other poles nobody wanted: the South Geomagnetic Pole, and the Pole of Inaccessibility.

Vostok was built on the first. On December sixteenth, nineteen fifty-seven, a tractor train arrived and set up camp, on flat snow, three and a half kilometres above sea level. That's about eleven thousand five hundred feet.
The nearest coast, at Mirny, was about fourteen hundred kilometres away. That's London to Rome, or Chicago to Denver. And there was no road. Only tracks in the snow.
The first winter, the thermometer fell to minus eighty-seven. In nineteen sixty, it reached minus eighty-eight point three, a world record.
That winter, the station chief, Vasily Sidorov, told reporters what the cold did. Diesel fuel turned into a sticky mass. Antifreeze crystallised. Metal became brittle.
Then the frame of the main diesel generator cracked. They could not weld it. At that height, there was not enough oxygen for the welding torch.
That was the first warning. At Vostok, the diesel is not just one machine. It's light, heat and water at once.

Even before the cold, there is the air. The station sits at three and a half thousand metres, but the polar air is so thin that your lungs think it's four thousand. There is nearly forty percent less oxygen in every breath.
New arrivals get headaches, dizziness, and trouble sleeping. A station doctor, Sergey Bushmanov, says people often lose five to ten kilos, ten to twenty pounds, in their first month.

Then the rules. At minus seventy and below, you may not stay outside for more than ten minutes. A mask is compulsory, because one deep breath can frostbite your airways. And at least half of every new crew must have wintered at Vostok before.
There is no liquid water here. Every drop starts as snow. The crew cuts blocks from a snow quarry, carries them inside, and melts them, with heat from the diesel.
And from late April to late August, the sun does not rise at all. That is when the real cold comes. In August, the average temperature is minus sixty-eight.
That's why the planes stop. From late February to mid-November, the air at Vostok stays below minus fifty-five. Too cold for any plane or tractor to come in.
So every summer, everything the station needs for winter has to arrive by road, fourteen hundred kilometres by tractor across the ice. Today the trains leave from Progress Station on the coast.
The tractors run on the same fuel they carry. About a third of it is burned on the way there.
And when the trains fail to bring enough, Vostok simply closes. It has been shut for the winter at least three times, because the fuel did not arrive.
So the whole station lives on one thing: diesel, turned into heat and light by one power station. And in nineteen eighty-two, that power station burned down.

In January nineteen eighty-two, the twenty-seventh Soviet expedition arrived at Vostok. Twenty-one men. Their leader was Pyotr Astakhov. He had led Vostok before, and Americans knew him. In nineteen sixty-seven, according to his biography, he climbed twenty-seven metres up a radio mast at the South Pole, at minus seventy, to fix an antenna. There's an Astakhov Glacier in Antarctica today.

In March, one of them fell ill. A plane flew in at below minus sixty to take him out. The doctor's notes call it the only flight like that in Vostok's history. Then the last plane left, and the winter began.
On April twelfth, a power technician, Sergei Kuznetsov, woke up to smoke. The fire probably started in the wiring of a small annex next to the machine hall, where the mechanics slept.
The head of the power station, Alexei Karpenko, went in to shut down the diesels. He died in the smoke.
The others threw snow and fired extinguishers. Nothing worked. The aluminium building melted. All the generators were lost.

But one thing went their way. The wind changed, and the flames missed the fuel store, dozens of barrels of diesel. The doctor, Arkady Maksimov, wrote later: without fuel, we would have had no chance of surviving.
Now the station was cold and dark, in the polar night, and nobody in the world knew.

A driller, Boris Moiseev, got a small generator from the drilling rig working. It was just enough for the radio. On the evening of April thirteenth, about sixteen hours after the fire, Vostok finally reached the outside world.
Evacuation was impossible. No plane could land, and no tractor could get through. So the men made a decision: they would stay, and finish the winter.
They found an old kerosene stove and heated the mess room. Then they made five stoves out of gas cylinders, burning diesel drip by drip.
Next to a stove, it was plus twenty-five at head height. Two metres away, by the wall, it was zero. They took turns at night to watch the fire.
They made candles from paraffin, with wicks of asbestos cord. They melted snow for water on the stoves. The cook baked bread by sticking the dough to the inside walls of a stove.
And the work went on. The meteorologist, Vello Park, kept up the full weather programme, every observation, even after his bosses cancelled all science at Vostok.
Outside, the winter fell to minus eighty-five.
Later, Moiseev revived an older generator from cold storage, so they had more power for light.
In early November, the first plane of spring flew in, with a new generator and four men from the next crew. About two weeks later, a tractor train arrived with materials for a new power station.
From the fire to the tractor train: two hundred and twenty-seven days.
Every man got a state award. Astakhov was nominated for Hero of the Soviet Union, but, by his biography's account, powerful people blocked it.
One year later, Vostok broke a record that still stands.
In July nineteen eighty-three, the next crew watched the temperature fall about two and a half degrees every day, for a week.

On July twenty-first, at five forty-five in the morning, Moscow time, the meteorologists on duty, Karpyuk and Lazarev, read the thermometer: minus eighty-nine point two. Minus a hundred and twenty-eight Fahrenheit.
That's seventy degrees Celsius colder than your freezer. And more than twenty degrees colder than the coldest towns where people live, like Oymyakon, in Siberia.
Scientists later found out why. For a whole week, there was no cloud and almost no wind, and a pool of the coldest air sat right over the station, with no warm air getting in.

Satellites have since seen colder spots: small hollows on the high ice ridge, where the snow surface reached about minus ninety-eight. But that is the snow, not the air. The coldest air ever measured is still Vostok's.
In a normal year, Vostok averages about minus fifty-five. By some estimates, that's about the average on Mars.
But the strangest thing about Vostok is not in the air. It's under the floor.

Under nearly four kilometres of ice, there is a lake. Lake Vostok is two hundred and forty kilometres long, nearly the size of Lake Ontario, kept liquid by the weight of the ice above it. Reaching it is why scientists put up with all this cold.

For decades, the crew drilled down, collecting ice. Russia, France and America drilled together, and split the ice three ways. The cores held air from more than four hundred thousand years ago. They showed that carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together, through four ice ages.

In twenty twelve, the drill finally reached the lake water. Did they find life? Reports of a new bacterium turned out to be contamination. A Russian geneticist, Vladimir Korolyov, put it bluntly: all of them were contaminants. So far, nothing alive has been confirmed.
So how do people survive at the coldest place ever measured?
Not with buildings alone. In nineteen eighty-two, the power station burned, and the men survived. And not with rescue. There was none.
Vostok survives on three things. Fuel, dragged fourteen hundred kilometres by tractor. A crew where half have done it before. And a spare for everything.

In nineteen eighty-two, Vostok had the fuel, and it had the people. What it didn't have was a spare. Light, heat and water all lived in one building. The only spares were the ones they dug out of the snow.

The new Vostok was built on that lesson. In January twenty twenty-four, a new winter complex started work: five blue modules, a hundred and forty metres long, longer than a football field, standing on thirty-six legs, so the snow blows underneath.
Its walls are eighty centimetres thick. It has a sauna, a gym and a cinema. It has four main generators. And two backup generators, in a separate module, far from the main power plant.
Getting it there took more than three years. The first ship broke a propeller off Angola and had to turn back. The modules finally crossed the ice by tractor, the same way as the fuel.
And at the end of every summer, the last plane still leaves, and the station is on its own again.
Would you spend one winter at Vostok, knowing that no plane can come for nine months? Tell me in the comments. And tell me which place we should explain next.

Alexei Karpenko is buried on a small island near Mirny, on the coast. And every April, when the last plane has gone and the sun goes down, the Vostok crew knows exactly what keeps them alive. It's a fire. The right kind of fire, in the right place, with a spare. This was How It's Run.
